¶
'''tundra''' (tön′drä̤), ''n.'' [Also ''toondra''; < Russ. ''tu'' ''dra'', a marshy plain.] In the northern part Russia (both in Europe and in Asia), one of tl nearly level treeless areas which occupy most that region, and do not differ essentially fro the steppes, except that, lying further nort their climate and vegetation are more decided arctic than those of the country to the sout with a corresponding increase in the numb of small lakes and morasses.

{{smaller block|A short distance south of Yefremov Kamen begins veritable ''tundra'', a woodless plain, interrupted by mountain heights, with small lakes scattered over it, narrow valleys crossing it, which often make an excurs on the apparently level plain extremely tiresome.
{{right|''Nordenskiöld'', Voyage of the Vega (trans.), I.}}}}

'''tundun''' (tun′dun), ''n.'' A toy: same as ''bull-roar''

'''tune''' (tūn), ''n.'' [< ME. ''tune'', < OF. ''ton'', F. ''ton'' Pr. ''ton'' = Sp. ''ton'', ''tono'' = It. ''tuono'', < L. ''ton'' < Gr. τόνος, a tone: see ''tone''<sup>1</sup>, of which ''tune'' i doublet.] '''1.''' A sound, especially a musi tone.
{{smaller block|<poem>Leave your betraying smiles,
And change the ''tunes'' of your enticing tongue
To penitential prayers.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''), Love’s Cure, ii}}}}

'''tune''' (tūn), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''tuned'', ppr. ''tunin'' [< ''tune'', ''n.'' Cf. ''attune.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To adjus the tones of (a voice or a musical instrument with reference to a correct or given standard pitch or temperament. See ''tuning''.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Tune'' your harps,
Ye angels, to that sound.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Spanish Friar, ii.}}}}
'''2.''' To play upon; produce melody or harmon from.
{{smaller block|<poem>When Orpheus ''tuned'' his lyre with pleasing woe,
Rivers forgot to run, and winds to blow.</poem>
{{right|''Addison'', Epil. to Granville’s British Enchante}}}}
'''3.''' To express by means of melody or harmon celebrate in music.
{{smaller block|<poem>Fountains, and ye that warble, as ye flow,
Melodious murmurs, warbling ''tune'' his praise.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., v. 1}}}}
'''4.''' To give a special tone or character to; a

'''tunefully''' (tūn′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' In a tuneful manner; harmoniously; musically.

'''tunefulness''' (tūn′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being tuneful.

'''tuneless''' (tūn′les), ''a.'' [< ''tune'' + ''-less.''] '''1.''' Unmusical; inharmonious.
readings.c3s1:
¶
'''2.''' Not employed in or not capable of making music.
{{smaller block|<poem>When in hand my ''tunelesse'' harp I take,
Then doe I more augment my foes despight.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Sonnets, xliv.}}}}

'''3.''' Not expressed rhythmically or musically; silent; without voice or utterance.
{{smaller block|<poem>On thy voiceless shore
The heroic lay is ''tuneless'' now;
The heroic bosom beats no more!</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Don Juan, iii. 86.}}}}

'''tuner''' (tū′nėr), ''n.'' [< ''tune'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' One who tunes or puts in tune; also, one who makes music or sings.
{{smaller block|The pox of such antic, lisping, affecting fantasticoes, these new ''tuners'' of accents! ''Shak.'', R. and J., ii. 4. 30.
<poem>Our mournful Philomel,
That rarest ''tuner''.</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Shepherd’s Sirena.}}}}

Specifically—'''2.''' One whose occupation it is to put musical instruments in proper tune and repair.
{{smaller block|There are a good many blind ''tuners''.
{{right|''J. H. Ewing'', Story of a Short Life, viii.}}}}

'''tungstite''' (tung′stīt), ''n.'' [< ''tungst''(''en'') + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.] Native oxid of tungsten, occurring in pulverulent form, of a bright-yellow color, usually in connection with wolfram, the tungstate of iron and manganese. Also called ''tungstic ocher.''

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|tun|6529|tungstite}}</noinclude>''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|My newe hous with the iij. ''tunnys'' of chemeneyis.
{{right|''Bury Wills'' (ed. Tymms), p. 20.}}}}

'''Bolt and tun''', in ''her.'' See ''bolt''<sup>1</sup>.

'''tun<sup>1</sup>''' (tun), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''tunned'', ppr. ''tunning.'' [< ''tun''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] '''1.''' To store in a tun or tuns, as wine or malt liquor; hence, to store in vessels of any sort for keeping.
{{smaller block|Amongst the rest with the apples of Adam; the juice whereof they ''tun'' up and send into Turky.
{{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 175.}}}}
'''2†.''' To fill as if a tun.
{{smaller block|<poem>A vale of tears, a vessel ''tunn’d'' with breath,
By sickness broach’d, to be drawn out by death.</poem>
{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, iii. 8.}}}}
'''3.''' To mingle with liquor when it is stored, as for the purpose of flavoring it, or making it keep better.
{{smaller block|The women of our northern parts do ''tun'' the herb alehouve into their ale.
{{right|''Gerard’s Herball'' (1579), quoted by Bickerdyke, p. 63.}}}}

'''tun<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''town.''

'''tuna<sup>1</sup>''' (tö′nä̤), ''n.'' A fish. See ''Thynnus'', ''Sarda'', ''Orcynus'', and ''tunny.''

'''tuna<sup>2</sup>''' (tū′nä̤), ''n.'' A species of prickly-pear, ''Opuntia Tuna'', or its fruit. {{smaller|It grows erect, sometimes 20 feet high, is spiny, and is much used for hedges in southern Europe. Its fruit, which is barrel-shaped and 2 or 3 inches long, is much eaten, fresh and dried. It is one of the foremost cochineal-plants, and is said to be the only species used for this production in the Canaries.}}

'''tunable''' (tū′na̤-bl), ''a.'' [Also ''tuneable''; < ''tune'' + ''-able.''] '''1.''' Capable of being put in tune, or made harmonious.
{{smaller block|God ringing the changes on all accidents, and making them ''tunable'' to His glory.
{{right|''Fuller'', Holy State, IV. xiii. 12}}}}

'''2.''' Harmonious; musical; tuneful. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|More ''tuneable'' than lark to shepherd’s ear.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., i. 1. 184.}}}}

'''tunableness''' (tū′na̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being tunable; harmony; melodiousness. Also ''tuneableness.''
{{smaller block|The ''tunableness'' and chiming of verse.
{{right|''Swift'', Advice to a Young Poet.}}}}

'''tunably''' (tū′na̤-bli), ''adv.'' In a tunable manner; harmoniously; musically. Also ''tuneably.''
{{smaller block|They can sing any thing most ''tunably'', Sir, but Psalms.
{{right|''Brome'', Jovial Crew,}}}}

'''tun-bellied†''' (tun′bel″id), ''a.'' Having a large protuberant belly; pot-bellied; paunchy.
{{smaller block|Their great huge rowling ''tunbellyed'' god Bacchus.
{{right|''Cartwright'', Royal Slave (1651). (''Nares.'')}}}}

'''tun-belly''' (tun′bel″i), ''n.'' A large protuberant belly.
{{smaller block|A double chin and a ''tun-belly.''
{{right|''Tom Brown'', Works, III. 152. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''tun-dish†''' (tun′dish), ''n.'' A funnel.
{{smaller block|Filling a bottle with a ''tun-dish.''
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iii. 2. 18}}}}

'''tundra''' (tön′drä̤), ''n.'' [Also ''toondra''; < Russ. ''tu'' ''dra'', a marshy plain.] In the northern part Russia (both in Europe and in Asia), one of tl nearly level treeless areas which occupy most that region, and do not differ essentially fro the steppes, except that, lying further nort their climate and vegetation are more decided arctic than those of the country to the sout with a corresponding increase in the numb of small lakes and morasses.

{{smaller block|A short distance south of Yefremov Kamen begins veritable ''tundra'', a woodless plain, interrupted by mountain heights, with small lakes scattered over it, narrow valleys crossing it, which often make an excurs on the apparently level plain extremely tiresome.
{{right|''Nordenskiöld'', Voyage of the Vega (trans.), I.}}}}

'''tundun''' (tun′dun), ''n.'' A toy: same as ''bull-roar''

'''tune''' (tūn), ''n.'' [< ME. ''tune'', < OF. ''ton'', F. ''ton'' Pr. ''ton'' = Sp. ''ton'', ''tono'' = It. ''tuono'', < L. ''ton'' < Gr. τόνος, a tone: see ''tone''<sup>1</sup>, of which ''tune'' i doublet.] '''1.''' A sound, especially a musi tone.
{{smaller block|<poem>Leave your betraying smiles,
And change the ''tunes'' of your enticing tongue
To penitential prayers.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''), Love’s Cure, ii}}}}
<poem>Whose senses in so evil consort their stepdame Nature
That ravishing delight in them most sweet ''tunes'' doth
raise.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I.}}}}

'''2.''' A well-rounded and pleasing successio tones; an air; a melody; especially, a b melodic piece in simple metrical form. term is often extended to include the harm with which such a melody is accompan Specifically—'''3.''' A musical setting of a hy usually in four-part harmony, intended for in public worship; a hymn-tune; chorale.— Same as ''entr’acte.'' Sometimes called an 410 tones in correct intonation; the proper construction or adjustment of a musical instrument with reference to such intonation; mutual adaptation of voices or instruments in pitch and temperament.
{{smaller block|<poem>Like sweet bells jangled, out of ''tune'' and harsh.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 1. 166.}}
A continual Parliament (I thought) would but keep the Common-weal in ''tune'', by preserving Laws in their due execution and vigour. {{right|''Eikon Basilike'', p. 27.}}}}
'''6.''' Frame of mind; mood; temper, especially temper for the time being: as, to be in ''tune'' (to be in the right disposition, or fit temper or humor).
{{smaller block|<poem>The poor distressed Lear ’s i’ the town;
Who sometime, in his better ''tune'', remembers
What we are come about.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 3. 41.}}}}
'''7.''' In ''phren.'', one of the perceptive faculties, of which the organ is said to be situated above the external angle of the orbit of the eye, as high as the middle of the forehead, on each side of the temporal ridge. This faculty is claimed to give the perception of melody or harmony. See ''phrenology''.—'''In tune''', {{smaller|in correct or properly adjusted intonation; harmonious.}}—'''Out of tune''', {{smaller|in incorrect or improperly adjusted intonation; inharmonious.}}—'''To change one’s tune''', {{smaller|to alter one’s manner and way of talking.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>O gin I live and bruik my life,
I’ll gar ye ''change your tune''.</poem>
{{right|''Wedding of Robin Hood and Little John'' (Child’s Ballads [V. 184).}}}}

'''To sing another tune.''' {{smaller|See ''sing''.}}—'''To the tune of''', {{smaller|to the sum or amount of. [Colloq.]}}

{{smaller block|Will Hazard has got the hipps, having lost ''to the tune o'' five hundr’d pound, tho’ he understands play very well, n body better.
{{right|''Swift'', Tatler, No. 23}}}}
'''tune''' (tūn), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''tuned'', ppr. ''tunin'' [< ''tune'', ''n.'' Cf. ''attune.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To adjus the tones of (a voice or a musical instrument with reference to a correct or given standard pitch or temperament. See ''tuning''.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Tune'' your harps,
Ye angels, to that sound.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Spanish Friar, ii.}}}}
'''2.''' To play upon; produce melody or harmon from.
{{smaller block|<poem>When Orpheus ''tuned'' his lyre with pleasing woe,
Rivers forgot to run, and winds to blow.</poem>
{{right|''Addison'', Epil. to Granville’s British Enchante}}}}
'''3.''' To express by means of melody or harmon celebrate in music.
{{smaller block|<poem>Fountains, and ye that warble, as ye flow,
Melodious murmurs, warbling ''tune'' his praise.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., v. 1}}}}
'''4.''' To give a special tone or character to; a tune.
{{smaller block|To that high-sounding Lyre I ''tune'' my Strains.
{{right|''Congreve'', Pindaric Odes,}}}}
{{smaller block|In peace, Love ''tunes'' the shepherd’s reed.
{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., iii.}}}}
'''5.''' To put into a state proper for any purpos or adapted to produce a particular effect.
{{smaller block|Come, let me ''tune'' you; glaze not thus your eyes
With self-love of a vow’d virginity.
{{right|''Massinger and Dekker'', Virgin-Martyr, ii}}}}
'''6.''' To bring into uniformity or harmony.
{{smaller block|Elizabeth might silence or ''tune'' the pulpits; but it impossible for her to silence or ''tune'' the great preach of justice, and mercy, and truth.
{{right|''J. R. Green'', Short Hist. Eng., p.}}}}
II. ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To give forth musical soun
{{smaller block|<poem>''Tuning'' to the water’s fall,
The small birds sang to her.</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Quest of Cynt}}}}
'''2.''' To accord with some correct or given sta dard of pitch or temperament.—'''3.''' To utter articulate musical sounds with the voice; s without using words; hum a tune. ''Imp. D'' [Rare.]—'''To tune up''', {{smaller|to begin to sing or play: birds ''tune up'' after a shower. [Colloq.]}}

'''tuneable, tuneableness''', etc. See ''tunable'', e

'''tuned''' (tūnd), ''a.'' [< ''tune'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Toned: u ally in composition: as, a shrill-''tuned'' bell.

'''tuneful''' (tūn′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ''tune'' + ''-ful.''] Full melody or tune. {{smaller|(''a'') Melodious; sweet of sound.}}
{{smaller block|The ''tuneful'' voice was heard from high.
{{right|''Dryden'', Song for St. Cecilia’s}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Producing sweet sounds; musical.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The Minstrel was infirm and old; . . .
His ''tuneful'' brethren all were dead.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M.,}}}}

'''tunefully''' (tūn′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' In a tuneful manner; harmoniously; musically.

'''tunefulness''' (tūn′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being tuneful.

'''tuneless''' (tūn′les), ''a.'' [< ''tune'' + ''-less.''] '''1.''' Unmusical; inharmonious.

'''2.''' Not employed in or not capable of making music.
{{smaller block|<poem>When in hand my ''tunelesse'' harp I take,
Then doe I more augment my foes despight.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Sonnets, xliv.}}}}

'''3.''' Not expressed rhythmically or musically; silent; without voice or utterance.
{{smaller block|<poem>On thy voiceless shore
The heroic lay is ''tuneless'' now;
The heroic bosom beats no more!</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Don Juan, iii. 86.}}}}

'''tuner''' (tū′nėr), ''n.'' [< ''tune'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' One who tunes or puts in tune; also, one who makes music or sings.
{{smaller block|The pox of such antic, lisping, affecting fantasticoes, these new ''tuners'' of accents! ''Shak.'', R. and J., ii. 4. 30.
<poem>Our mournful Philomel,
That rarest ''tuner''.</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Shepherd’s Sirena.}}}}

Specifically—'''2.''' One whose occupation it is to put musical instruments in proper tune and repair.
{{smaller block|There are a good many blind ''tuners''.
{{right|''J. H. Ewing'', Story of a Short Life, viii.}}}} '''3.''' In ''organ-building'', an adjustable flap or opening near the top of a flue-pipe, whereby the effective length of the air-column may be altered, so as to alter the pitch of the tone.

'''tung†''', ''n.'' An old spelling of ''tongue.''

'''tung-oil''' (tung′oil), ''n.'' [< Chinese ''t’ung'' + E. ''oil.''] A fixed oil obtained from the seeds of the tung-tree, ''Aleurites cordata'', forming 35 per cent. of their weight. {{smaller|It is produced in immense quantities in China, where it is universally employed for calking and painting junks and boats, and for varnishing and preserving all kinds of woodwork. In drying quality it surpasses all other known oils. It is also used for lighting, but is inferior for the purpose to tea-oil. It is not known in European commerce. Also ''tree-oil'' or ''wood-oil.'' ''Spons’ Encyc. Manuf.''}}

'''tun-great†''' (tun′grāt), ''a.'' [ME. ''tonne greet;'' < ''tun''<sup>1</sup> + ''great.''] Having a circumference of the size of a tun.
{{smaller block|<poem>Every piler, the temple to sustene,
Was ''tonne-greet,'' of iren bright and shene.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 1136.}}}}

'''tungstate''' (tung′stāt), ''n.'' [< ''tungst(ic)'' + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] A salt of tungstic acid: as, ''tungstate'' of lime.—{{smaller|'''Sodium tungstate''', a crystalline salt prepared by roasting wolfram with soda-ash. It is used as a mordant, and to render fabrics uninflammable.}}

'''tungsten''' (tung′sten), ''n.'' [= F. ''tungstène'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''tungsteno'' = G. ''tungstein'', < Sw. ''tungsten'' (= Dan. ''tungsteen''), < ''tung'', heavy, = Dan. ''tung'' = Icel. ''thungr'', heavy (cf. ''thungi'', a load, ''thunga'', load), + ''sten'', stone, = Dan. ''steen'' = G. ''stein'' = E. ''stone'', q. v.] '''1.''' Chemical symbol, W; atomic weight, 183.5. A metal some of whose ores have long been known (see ''wolfram'' and ''scheelite''), but they were supposed to be compounds of tin. {{smaller block|That scheelite (tungstate of lime) was a compound of lime with a peculiar metallic acid was proved by Scheele and Bergman in 1781, and the composition of wolfram was also determined by the brothers D’Elhujar a few years later. Metallic tungsten, as obtained by the reduction of the trioxid, is a gray powder having a metallic luster and a specific gravity of 19.129 (Roscoe). The most interesting fact in regard to tungsten is that tungsteniferous minerals, especially wolfram, are very frequent associates of the ores of tin. (See ''wolfram.'') Tungsten has been experimented with in various ways, as in improving the quality of steel by being added to it in small quantity; but no alloy containing tungsten has come into general use. (See ''tungsten steel'', under ''steel''<sup>1</sup>.) A new alloy called ''sideraphite'', containing a large percentage of iron, with some nickel, aluminium, and copper, together with 4 per cent. of tungsten, has recently been introduced; this is said to resemble silver, and to be very ductile and malleable and not easily attacked by acids. Another alloy called ''minargent'', consisting chiefly of copper and nickel, is said sometimes to contain a small percentage of tungsten. Tungsten is chemically related to molybdenum and uranium. Certain chemically remarkable compounds of tungsten (tungstates with tungsten dioxid) have been employed as substitutes for bronze-powder.}}
'''2.''' The native tungstate of lime.—'''Tungsten steel.''' {{smaller|See ''steel''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''tungstenic''' (tung-sten′ik), ''a.'' [< ''tungsten'' + ''-ic.''] Of or pertaining to or procured from tungsten; tungstic.

'''tungsteniferous''' (tung-sten-if′e-rus), ''a.'' Containing tungsten.

'''tungstic''' (tung′stik), ''a.'' [< ''tungst(en)'' + ''-ic.''] Of or pertaining to or obtained from tungsten. {{smaller|—'''Tungstic acid''', an acid obtained by precipitating a solution of tungstic oxid in an alkali by the addition of an acid. It is dibasic, having the composition H<sub>2</sub>WO<sub>4</sub>.—}}

'''Tungstic ocher.''' Same as ''tungstite.''

'''tungstite''' (tung′stīt), ''n.'' [< ''tungst''(''en'') + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.] Native oxid of tungsten, occurring in pulverulent form, of a bright-yellow color, usually in connection with wolfram, the tungstate of iron and manganese. Also called ''tungstic ocher.''<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
